migrationNotes: Spine: one empty box in a pupil survey, followed through counting, adding, averaging and picking the smallest, then filled with a zero, and finally a question that leaves no rows at all.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-aggregate-known-values-8 (COUNT(*) as a choice) and -9 (why AVG divides by one). Both ideas are taught on the first and third screens and asked again in the skill check.

lesson.title: Choose the right denominator

lead.text: Put the survey in a table, with one row for each pupil and a column for the number of books. The fourth pupil's cell is empty, which in SQL is NULL: a value nobody knows. A function that reads many rows and returns a single value is called an aggregate, and COUNT is the simplest one to start with.

COUNT comes in two forms that give different answers. COUNT(*) counts rows, so it counts every pupil whether or not the box was filled in. COUNT(books) counts the values in one column and skips the NULLs, so it counts only the pupils who gave an answer. The picture runs both on the survey.

afterFigure.text: The first query finds four pupils and the second finds three answers. The gap between the two numbers is how a missing value shows up. Every aggregate that reads a column behaves in this way: it looks at the known values and passes over the NULLs, as if those rows were absent for that column. The next screens ask what that means for totals, averages and the smallest and largest value.

queries.label: Count every pupil
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS pupils FROM survey;

queries.label: Count the answers
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(books) AS answers FROM survey;

lead.text: The shop's orders table has six rows, and the amount of order 106 is unknown. Compare counting the rows with counting the amount column.

reveal.text: You left out the unknown amount, so the column count came out one short of the row count. That gap is how a missing value shows.

queries.label: Count every order
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders;

queries.label: Count known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders;

lead.text: SUM and AVG pass over the empty box just as COUNT(books) did. SUM adds the values that are known. AVG adds the same values and then divides by how many there were, so the number it divides by is the count of known values and not the count of rows.

The shop's orders show it in a small case. Customer 3 has orders 105 and 106, and the amount of order 106 is unknown. Their SUM(amount) is 20, because there is only one known amount to add. Their AVG(amount) is also 20, because that one amount is divided by one and not by two. The second query in the picture counts the rows and the known amounts, so the number being divided by is on show.

afterFigure.text: An average of the known values describes the orders whose amounts we know. It says nothing about the order with the empty amount, and it is not what you would get by dividing by every order. Both numbers are honest answers to different questions, and a later screen shows how to ask for the second one. For now, remember that AVG divides by COUNT(column) and never by COUNT(*).

queries.label: Sum and average
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

queries.label: Rows and known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

lead.text: Work this one out by hand, the way AVG would.

MIN and MAX pick the smallest and the largest value in a column, and they pass over NULL like the others. An empty cell cannot be the smallest value because it holds no value at all. Reading it as a zero and expecting MIN to find it would be a mistake.

A WHERE clause runs before the aggregate and decides which rows it gets to see. Ask for MIN(amount) with a WHERE test and the function looks only at the rows that passed, and the same goes for MAX. So the order of work is to filter the rows first and then pick from what is left.

afterFigure.text: The picture runs MIN and MAX on all six orders and then on customer 3's two orders. One of those two orders has no amount, and both functions report 20, the only amount there is. The unknown order was not chosen as the smallest, and it did not drag the minimum down to zero.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS smallest, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders;

queries.label: Customer 3 only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS smallest, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 3;

lead.text: Pending orders are the ones whose status says pending. Filter first, then let MIN pick from the amounts that are left.

reveal.text: You picked from the known amounts of the filtered rows. An unknown amount never stands in for a smallest value.

queries.label: All orders
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders;

queries.label: Pending only
queries.sql: SELECT MIN(amount) AS minimum, MAX(amount) AS maximum FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

lead.text: Leaving unknown values out is what an aggregate does unless it is told otherwise, and sometimes that is the wrong reading. If an empty box in the books column really means the pupil read nothing, the average ought to count that pupil.

COALESCE does the telling. COALESCE(books, 0) returns books when it is known and 0 when it is NULL, so wrapping a column in it fills every gap with 0 before the aggregate looks. AVG(COALESCE(books, 0)) then adds 4, 6, 8 and 0, and divides by 4, because the zero is now a value that counts.

afterFigure.text: On the survey that gives 4.5 and not 6. The data has not changed, only the question. 6 is the average among the pupils who answered, and 4.5 is the average if the pupil who didn't answer is taken to have read nothing. Neither is wrong, so decide which one you mean before you write the query.

queries.label: Known answers only
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(books) AS mean FROM survey;

queries.label: Blank counted as zero
queries.sql: SELECT AVG(COALESCE(books, 0)) AS mean FROM survey;

lead.text: Back to the shop's six orders, with one amount unknown. The query asks for the plain average, with nothing filled in.

reveal.text: You divided by the known amounts only. The unknown amount neither adds to the total nor counts as an order.

queries.label: Keep missing separate
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: Fill missing with zero
queries.sql: SELECT SUM(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS total, AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0)) AS mean FROM orders;

lead.text: One case remains. A WHERE clause can remove every row, and a query that uses an aggregate still returns exactly one row, because the question still has to be answered. COUNT(*) has an easy answer: it found no rows, so it says 0.

The others have a harder time. AVG has nothing to add up and nothing to divide by, and MAX has no value to pick, so each of them reports NULL, meaning there is no result to give. COUNT is the odd one out because a count of nothing is a real number.

afterFigure.text: The picture asks for the count, the average and the largest amount among orders over 100, and there are no such orders. The answer comes back as one row holding 0, NULL and NULL. This matters when a report is built from filtered rows, because a NULL in the result can mean that nothing matched and not that the data is damaged.

queries.label: All six orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, AVG(amount) AS mean, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders;

queries.label: Amounts over 100
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, AVG(amount) AS mean, MAX(amount) AS largest FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lead.text: The last screen left SUM out. When WHERE leaves no rows at all, decide what the total of those rows should be.

queries.label: Known orders
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders;

queries.label: No matches
queries.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS total, AVG(amount) AS mean FROM orders WHERE amount > 100;

lesson.orientation: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX while keeping missing values visible.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four pupils were asked how many books they read this month. Three of them answered: 4, 6 and 8. The fourth handed the form back with the box empty.

The teacher wants one number for the whole class, an average, so there is a decision to make about the empty box. Treating it as a zero says that pupil read nothing, which nobody knows. Leaving the pupil out says the class has three pupils in it, which isn't true either. The two choices give different averages, and the choice matters whether you work the figure out by hand or ask a database to do it.

A query that boils many rows down to one figure meets the same empty box every time it reaches a value nobody recorded. This lesson follows that one empty box through counting, adding, averaging and picking the smallest, to see what the database does with it and how to change that when you want to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll know which rows each summary counts, and what an unknown value does to a total or an average.

recap.keyIdea: An aggregate reads only the known values, so COUNT(column), SUM and AVG leave unknowns out of both the sum and the count, and COALESCE fills the gaps first when you want them counted.

blocks.text: You worked out an average of 6 from three answers and 48 from the shop's five known amounts. The 6 fell to 4.5 once the empty box counted as a zero. With no rows left to add, SUM came back NULL.

recap.nextHook: One average for a whole table is only the start. A café owner with a pile of slips wants a figure for each drink, and that means summarising each pile on its own.

questions.prompt: What does COUNT(amount) return for the shop's six orders?
hints: Count known values in the column.
COUNT(amount) excludes the NULL row.
Order 106 has no known amount; inspect the amounts on all the other orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five rows have a non-NULL amount; order 106 is missing.

questions.onCorrect: 5. COUNT(amount) counts the known amounts, so the unknown one is left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows, which COUNT(*) gives. COUNT(amount) skips the unknown amount.

questions.prompt: What is AVG(amount) for the shop's six orders?
hints: Add only known amounts.
Use the count of known amounts as the denominator.
Evaluate 240 ÷ 5; NULL is outside this denominator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known total is 240 across five known amounts: 240 ÷ 5 = 48.

questions.onCorrect: 48. SUM adds the known amounts, and AVG divides by how many there are.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by all six rows, as if the unknown amount were a zero.
That is the total. AVG divides it by the number of known amounts.

questions.prompt: What is MIN(amount) for pending orders?
hints: Filter to pending orders first.
Ignore the missing amount; do not replace it with zero.
The pending amounts are a known value on order 104 and NULL on order 106; only the known value participates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Order 104 is the only pending order with a known amount; MIN is 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. WHERE keeps the pending orders, and MIN ignores the unknown amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The unknown amount is not a zero. MIN ignores it.
That is the smallest amount over all orders. Filter to pending orders first.

questions.prompt: With no matching rows, type the value SUM(amount) returns in SQLite.
hints: No observed sum is different from a known zero sum.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SQLite SUM(amount) returns NULL when there are no non-NULL input values, including an empty matching set. COUNT instead returns zero for an empty set.

questions.onCorrect: NULL. With no rows to add, SUM has no total to report, which is not the same as zero.

misconceptions.feedback: A total of zero would claim that rows were added up. With no rows there is no total.

questions.prompt: Known values are 10 and 30, with one NULL. What does AVG(value) return?
hints: The missing value does not add to the count.
Divide the known total by two.
Evaluate (10 + 30) ÷ 2; the missing observation is excluded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AVG uses the two known values: (10 + 30) ÷ 2 = 20.

questions.onCorrect: 20. The unknown value is out of the sum and the count, so it is 40 ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by three, counting the unknown value. AVG leaves it out.
That is the total. AVG divides it by the number of known values.

questions.prompt: What changes when you use AVG(COALESCE(amount, 0))?
hints: The replacement becomes an input value to AVG.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COALESCE replaces each missing amount with zero before averaging. Those rows now contribute to the denominator, which can change the average.

questions.onCorrect: Missing amounts count as zeros. COALESCE replaces NULL before AVG sees it, so the count rises.

misconceptions.feedback: COALESCE fills the gap before AVG runs, so the gaps no longer disappear.
The values AVG reads change as well, so the average can change.

questions.prompt: Four pupils were asked how many books they read this month. Three answered 4, 6 and 8. The fourth left the box empty. What is the average of the answers?
hints: Which pupils should count towards the average?
Add up the numbers that were reported.
Divide by the number of answers, not the number of pupils.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The answers are 4, 6 and 8. They add up to 18, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The pupil who did not answer adds nothing and is not counted. AVG treats an unknown value the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by all four pupils. The one who did not answer gave no number to include.

questions.prompt: Which one counts every row, including rows with an unknown amount?
hints: Which one does not look at a single column?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(amount) counts only rows where amount is known.

questions.onCorrect: COUNT(*) counts rows. Counting a column counts only its known values.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts known amounts only, so a row with an unknown amount is left out.
SUM adds amounts. It does not count rows.

questions.prompt: Why does AVG(amount) divide by one here, not two?
hints: How many of the two amounts are known?

acceptedIdeas: AVG counts only the known amounts.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One of the two amounts is unknown, and AVG leaves it out of both the sum and the count.

questions.onCorrect: AVG skips unknown values in the sum and in the count, so it divides by the known amounts only.

choices.label: AVG counts only the known amounts.
AVG treats the unknown amount as zero.

misconceptions.feedback: Then it would divide by both orders. AVG skips unknown values instead.
Nothing says it was cancelled. Its amount is simply not known.

questions.prompt: A column holds 5, NULL, 7 and 8. What does COUNT(column) return?
hints: Does COUNT(column) count the unknown value?
Count the values that are known.
Four rows, minus the unknown one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three of the four values are known, so COUNT(column) is three.

questions.onCorrect: 3. COUNT on a column counts known values, so the NULL is left out.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts rows. COUNT(column) skips the unknown value.
